report:
## Conclusion

Yes — denosumab (Prolia) substantially reduces the risk of vertebral fractures in patients with osteoporosis, and this effect is well established by high-quality randomized controlled trial evidence.

The pivotal FREEDOM trial, a 3-year, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study in postmenopausal women with osteoporosis, found that twice-yearly subcutaneous denosumab reduced new radiographic vertebral fractures from 7.2% (placebo) to 2.3% (denosumab) — a 68% relative risk reduction (p<0.001) — along with reductions in nonvertebral and hip fractures (NEJM, https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/nejmoa0809493). This benefit persisted and was sustained over 10 years of continuous treatment in the FREEDOM Extension study, with progressive BMD gains and continued low vertebral fracture rates (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8799550/). Similar large relative risk reductions (e.g., ~68% in Japanese cohorts) have been confirmed in other populations (DIRECT trial data, https://www.academia.edu/14092057/Fracture_Risk_Reduction_with_Denosumab_in_Japanese_Postmenopausal_Women_and_Men_with_Osteoporosis_Denosumab_fracture_Intervention_RandomizEd_placebo_Controlled_Trial_DIRECT_).

An important caveat: the anti-fracture benefit is dependent on continued treatment. Discontinuing denosumab causes a rebound increase in bone turnover and rapid bone loss, which is associated with an increased risk of multiple vertebral fractures, particularly in patients with a prior vertebral fracture (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3617467/). Clinicians therefore recommend transitioning promptly to an alternative antiresorptive agent if denosumab is stopped.

**Bottom line:** Denosumab is effective and well-supported for reducing vertebral fracture risk in osteoporosis when taken continuously as prescribed, but abrupt discontinuation can negate this benefit and increase fracture risk.
